Chapter One. Darkness

Introduction to the dark coast

Before the lanterns there was the coast itself, a long ragged line of rock that the harbour records describe as unlit for most of the year, and a road that ran beside it through four villages.

The keepers wrote to one another constantly. Their letters are the main source for this chapter,1 and they are full of complaints about oil, wicks and the price of glass.

The road is described again in the introduction, and the method in the method section, which this page does not have.

One keeper, writing in the second winter, said that the dark was not the absence of light but the presence of weather,2 and that every lantern was an argument with the wind.

Older editions of the letters numbered them by village rather than by date, which makes the sequence of the first winter hard to follow without a map of the road.

By the end of the first winter four lanterns stood on the coast road, one for each village, and the letters begin to talk about the light rather than the dark.

Notes

  1. Ibid.↩︎

  2. Letter of the second winter, from the keeper at the northern village.↩︎
